newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan, HK activists get scant support in Japan row.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan, HK activists get scant support in Japan row.

text.p: Japan's success in blocking a Chinese nationalist flotilla from reaching a disputed East China Sea archipelago took the wind out of protesters' sails and sent them scurrying home to find little support.
Taiwan activists who led the failed mission to challenge Japan's claim to the islets returned home on Tuesday to hear their government talking tough to Tokyo -- but promising no action.
Worse yet, an anti-Japan egg-throwing rally they organised in Taipei drew fewer than 20 people.

Their colleagues in Hong Kong fared even worse, mustering a measly five participants for an anti-Japanese protest while the British colony's newspapers brushed off the mission as misguided and downright unnecessary.

Tokyo on Monday deployed 60 patrol ships, some armed, and used their superior numbers to keep a 20-boat flotilla of Chinese nationalists away from the islets, held by Japan as the Senkakus but claimed by Taiwan and China as the Diaoyus.
Japan's claim to the islands has fuelled nationalist passion in Chinese communities in Hong Kong, Taiwan and North America since Japanese rightists built a lighthouse there in July 1996.

Despite some minor collisions on Monday, Japan's coast guard showed firmness and restraint as they hemmed in the protest boats to keep them away from the unpopulated outcrops, lying 200 km (125 miles) northeast of Taiwan and southwest of Japan's Okinawa island chain.
The Japanese refrained from arresting several protesters who jumped aboard their patrol boats in what appeared to be attempts to incite embarrassing confrontations.
Japan's successful strategy appeared to have won tacit approval in Taiwan and Hong Kong as protesters returned to cool responses at home on Tuesday.

In Taipei, fewer than 20 demonstrators appeared outside Tokyo's mission to hurl eggs and burn Japanese flags. The rally soon dissipated after the activists failed to penetrate a cordon of Taiwan police protecting the building.
Taipei's foreign ministry issued a strong protest to Tokyo's unofficial office, saying Taiwan was "very dissatisfied with Japan's violation of our country's sovereignty".
But Taipei showed no intention of putting teeth behind its protest. Instead, it urged activists not to provoke conflict.
Communist China likewise took a low-key approach.

In Beijing, Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofeng issued a vague call for Tokyo to "adopt truly effective measures" and sidestepped a question on whether Beijing would help activists seek compensation from Tokyo.
In Hong Hong, just five people turned up for a rally outside China's diplomatic outpost to demand tougher anti-Japan action by Beijing, which takes the British colony's reins in July.
Local media offered no succour. Hong Kong's English-language South China Morning Post said support for the activists' cause was "evaporating, in part because of their own conduct".
The activists had taken up matters "totally outside their capacity", the Post said in its editorial.
In Japan, Tokyo restated its claim to the uninhabited islets and defended the emphatic rebuff it dealt to the demonstrators.
"We deeply regret the fact that some of the protest ships entered Japan's territorial waters," Transport Minister Makoto Koga told reporters.
"But I would like to thank the Maritime Safety Agency and other ministries concerned for being able to block them (the activists) from landing on the islands," Koga said.

Japan took the chain as war booty after defeating imperial China in 1895. Despite deep differences, China and Taiwan agree the islands should have been returned to Chinese control after Japan's World War Two defeat.
